gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own Elite 200 V2 + 2× 200 W kit uses only 400 W of the station's 1,000 W (12–60 V, 20 A) solar input, or that a third SP200L panel can't simply be added in series (3 × 26.1 V Voc = 78.3 V, over the 60 V limit). In good sun the kit's two panels give about 300–340 W, so the 2.44 kWh StorageReview measured to refill an empty Elite 200 V2 takes roughly 7–8 hours of full sun, not the 2.4 hours BLUETTI quotes for its 1,000 W maximum.
standout_why: I compared against backuppowerhub.com/best-power-station-for-refrigerator-backup (lists solar input watts but says nothing on Voc, series/parallel wiring or solar refill time; the Elite 200 V2 appears only in its 'Also worth a look' section) and solarpowerauditor.com/home-backup/best-power-station-home-backup (gives a 2×100 W solar refill time of 13 h 49 min for the Elite 200 V2 but no voltage window or panel-count limit, and nothing on the BLUETTI SP200L kit). Neither page covers how the panels in the kit fit the station's voltage and current limits, or how long the actual kit takes to refill. That decides how many panels, and which panel, go in the cart. Partial overlap: backuppowerhub has its own SP200L review (not in ChatGPT's results) saying series wiring is 'not recommended' for some BLUETTI stations, but it does not do the Elite 200 V2 arithmetic.
kit_items: Power station: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. 2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 and 2,600 W continuous (BLUETTI). Measured usable output is 1,902 Wh (Solar Power Auditor) or 1.91 kWh (StorageReview). A 500 kWh/yr fridge averages 500 ÷ 8.76 ≈ 57 W, so 1,902 Wh ÷ 57 W ≈ 33 h on the fridge alone.

Solar: 2× BLUETTI SP200L 200 W panels, bought as the store's Elite 200 V2 + 2×200W bundle. Two in parallel (about 18 A) or two in series (52.2 V Voc) both stay inside the 12–60 V / 20 A input. The 400 W of panels uses 40% of the 1,000 W input, so plan for about one full sunny day per refill.

Wall charging: the built-in 1,800 W AC input. 1,800 W ÷ 120 V = 15 A, the full rating of a typical 15 A household circuit, so charge it on a circuit with nothing else heavy running. StorageReview measured 2.44 kWh drawn to put back 1.91 kWh (about 78% round trip).
